title: Le rôle des compétences managériales numériques et éthiques dans le développement de la responsabilité numérique des entreprises : proposition d'un cadre conceptuel
summary: RésuméLa transformation numérique place les entreprises devant des responsabilités qui dépassent la conformité technique : protection des données, sécurité des systèmes, équité des décisions automatisées, accessibilité, transparence et sobriété. La responsabilité numérique des entreprises (RNE), traduction retenue ici de Corporate Digital Responsibility (CDR), désigne l’orientation qui encadre ces usages, tandis que les pratiques de RNE en constituent la traduction observable. Les cadres existants ont éclairé les principes, les activités et les niveaux de responsabilité, mais explicitent de manière inégale la contribution conjointe des compétences numériques et éthiques des managers aux mécanismes organisationnels qui permettent leur mise en œuvre. La question posée est la suivante : comment et par quels mécanismes les compétences managériales numériques et éthiquespeuvent-elles favoriser les pratiques de RNE ? L’étude propose une synthèse narrative à visée conceptuelle fondée sur les travaux académiques et les référentiels institutionnels cités, complétée par une actualisation bibliographique ciblée jusqu’en octobre 2026. La démarche privilégie l’analyse critique des travaux et la construction de relations théoriques, conformément aux objectifs d’une revue narrative à visée conceptuelle. Deux familles de compétences sont articulées aux arrangements de gouvernance numérique responsable et à la culture éthique numérique. Ces deux mécanismes sont considérés comme des médiateurs partiels potentiels, sans exclure des trajectoires croisées. La maturité numérique et la pression des parties prenantes sont envisagées comme conditions contextuelles, et non comme effets démontrés. Le cadre formule huit propositions derecherche et distingue les compétences au niveau des managers, les mécanismes collectifs et les pratiques à l’échelle de l’organisation. Il propose ainsi une explication testable du passage des dispositions individuelles aux routines responsables, tout en précisant ses limites : portée conceptuelle des propositions, sélection raisonnée des références et possibilité de relations réciproques. Des voies de vérification par enquêtes multiniveaux, études de cas et analyses longitudinales sont discutées. AbstractDigital transformation confronts organizations with responsibilities that extend beyond technical compliance, including data protection, cyber resilience, fairness in automated decisions, accessibility, transparency and digital sustainability. Corporate digital responsibility (CDR) refers here to the values and norms guiding responsible digital practices, while CDR practices refer to their observable implementation. Existing frameworks have clarified principles, activities and levels of responsibility, yet they offer uneven explanations of how managers’ digital and ethical capabilities jointly become organizational mechanisms supporting implementation. This paper asks: how, and through which organizational mechanisms, can digital and ethical managerial competencies foster CDR practices? It develops a conceptual model through a narrative, theory-oriented synthesis of the academic and institutional materials cited in the paper, complemented by a targeted bibliographic update through October 2026. The narrative synthesis uses a reasoned selection of academic and institutional sources to compare theoretical perspectives and articulate a testable conceptual framework. The framework connects two families of managerial competencies with responsible digital governance and a digital ethical culture. These are proposed as potentially partial mediators, while cross-pathways remain plausible. Digital maturity and stakeholder pressure are discussed as contextual moderators whose effects must be tested rather than assumed. Eight research propositions distinguish individual managerial resources from collective organizational mechanisms and organizational-level responsible practices. The article distinctive contribution isnot to establish causal effects, but to specify a testable explanation of the translation of managerial judgment and digital literacy into rules, shared routines, monitoring and stakeholder-responsive actions. It also makes explicit the risks of construct overlap, reverse causality and different regulatory environments. Future testing could combine multilevel surveys, longitudinal observations and case studies with structural equation and conditional-process analyses. The proposed relationships form a theoretical research agenda and remain open to empirical examination and competing explanations.

title: Adoption of the Fintech Services among Young Entrepreneurs
summary: The rapid development of financial technology (FinTech) has transformed the delivery and utilisation of financial services, creating new opportunities for entrepreneurs to conduct business transactions, manage finances and access digital financial solutions. Young entrepreneurs represent an important segment of the entrepreneurial ecosystem because of their potential to promote innovation, employment generation and economic development. The adoption of FinTech services can help them improve transaction efficiency, maintain financial records and manage business activities more conveniently. However, the extent of adoption may depend on technological capabilities, financial knowledge, perceived benefits, accessibility, trust and security concerns. Against this background, the present study, titled “Adoption of FinTech Services Among Young Entrepreneurs,” aims to examine the adoption patterns and preferences of FinTech services and analyse the factors influencing their adoption. The study focuses on digital payments, mobile banking, internet banking, digital wallets and online lending platforms. It considers digital literacy, financial literacy, perceived usefulness, ease of use, trust, accessibility and security concerns as potential determinants of FinTech adoption. A descriptive research design is proposed, with primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to young entrepreneurs. A sample of 100 respondents may be considered, subject to the availability of participants and the defined scope of the study. Secondary data may be obtained from academic journals, research articles, books and relevant institutional reports. Frequency and percentage analysis, mean scores, standard deviation and correlation analysis may be used to examine the data. Multiple regression may also be employed to identify the relative contribution of selected factors to FinTech adoption. The illustrative analysis presented for this study suggests that digital payments and mobile banking may be widely used by young entrepreneurs, while online lending platforms may have comparatively lower adoption. Perceived usefulness, ease of use and accessibility emerge as important factors to investigate, while trust and security remain relevant considerations. These preliminary, illustrative patterns are not empirical findings and must be verified using actual survey data. The study is expected to provide insights for FinTech service providers, policymakers and entrepreneurship-support organisations in developing accessible, secure and user-friendly financial solutions. It also emphasises the importance of digital and financial literacy in promoting informed and responsible adoption of FinTech services among young entrepreneurs..

title: Multi-Objective Constrained Deep Q-Networks for Supplier Selection and Order Allocation in Sustainable Supply Chains
summary: Abstract Sustainable sourcing requires sequential decisions that couple discrete supplier admission, integer order quantities, stochastic lead times, inventory, and competing economic, environmental, and service objectives. We formulate this setting as a preference-conditioned constrained Markov decision process with state-dependent, mixed-integer action feasibility and distributional tail-risk requirements. We develop ParetoShield-Q, a multi-objective deep Q-learning formulation that uses an augmented Chebyshev action functional over distributional cost-to-go estimates and a completion-feasibility oracle to construct executable supplier allocations. The same constrained Bellman operator jointly determines which objectives are optimized, which downstream risks are penalized, and which supplier--quantity assignments are legally selectable. We establish conditional one-step feasibility and finite-candidate Pareto-efficiency properties, and provide an evaluation protocol based on the public M5 demand data and a public supplier-attribute dataset. The study presents seven quantitative tables and eight vector figures spanning multi-objective performance, preference control, cost composition, operational feasibility, ablations, disruption response, and computational scaling. The visualizations reproduce the tabulated numerical summaries without constructing unobserved run-level training traces. Independent reproduction requires the source training runs, scenario configurations, and optimizer logs.

title: Greenhushing as Strategic Adaptation: Net‐Zero Commitment Retreat Among S&P 500 Firms Amid Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) Backlash
summary: ABSTRACT Greenhushing has emerged as a strategic corporate response to political and regulatory uncertainty, yet less is known about how firms recalibrate previously established sustainability signals when external conditions change. Drawing on signaling theory, this study examines changes in corporate climate and ESG commitments during the political transition to the second Trump administration. Using qualitative content analysis of corporate disclosures and public communications, we identify 32 large US firms that modified, weakened, or withdrew previously stated commitments between September 2024 and August 2025. Among these firms, 13 (41%) were associated with political or regulatory pressure, 8 (25%) linked changes to rising AI and data‐center demand, and 11 (34%) pointed to profit‐driven refocusing, market uncertainty, or broader regulatory ambiguity. The findings reveal clear sectoral differences in how firms recalibrated sustainability signals. Financial institutions exhibited the most direct and visible retrenchment, particularly through withdrawals from net‐zero alliances and changes in ESG‐related communication. Technology firms more often retained long‐term climate commitments while reducing the visibility, prominence, or certainty of interim targets. Other sectors showed less visible but still consequential forms of retreat, including target modification and the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) delisting. Case studies of BlackRock, Meta, and Microsoft further identify three distinct pathways of greenhushing: politically induced retrenchment, selective undercommunication amid rising emissions, and more cautious or conditional sustainability signaling in response to reputational and regulatory risk.

title: ESG Controversies and Short‐Term Profitability: The Role of Current ESG Performance and Lagged Reputation in Emerging Markets
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines whether ESG controversy involvement is associated with short‐term return on equity (ROE) and whether current and lagged ESG scores moderate that relationship among Indian nonfinancial firms. Drawing on stakeholder theory, legitimacy theory, and the managerial opportunism hypothesis, the study analyses 382 NIFTY 500 firm‐year observations for FY2024–25 using Hayes PROCESS Macro moderation models, with PLS‐SEM employed as a robustness check. ESG controversy involvement is positively associated with ROE, an association consistent with transitory cost externalization under India's formative mandatory disclosure environment. Current ESG scores significantly attenuate the controversy–ROE association, with positive associations concentrated among low‐ESG firms rather than consistently observed across all firms, providing conditional support for the managerial opportunism hypothesis. This moderating pattern is corroborated across estimation approaches. In contrast, ESG scores measured one and 2 years prior do not exhibit consistent additional moderation beyond current ESG performance. As controversy involvement and ROE are observed only for FY2024–25, the findings do not establish temporal adjustment, persistence, or changes in the financial consequences of controversies over time. The study contributes by distinguishing the moderating roles of current and prior ESG standing, identifying the conditional nature of the controversy–profitability association among NIFTY 500 non‐financial firms, and extending the managerial opportunism hypothesis to an emerging‐market regulatory context.

title: Digital Transformation and Sustainable Development of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in South East, Nigeria
summary: This study examined the effect of digital transformation on the sustainable development of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in South East Nigeria, focusing on digital business process integration and economic sustainability, as well as digital infrastructure adoption and social sustainability. The study was motivated by the increasing importance of digital technologies driven by the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) and the need for SMEs to achieve long-term sustainability in business operations amidst the challenges facing SMEs in achieving sustainable development in emerging economies. The study was anchored on Resource-Based View (RBV) Theory and adopted a survey research design. The population comprised of 10,016 employees of selected registered SMEs, based on their involvement in business activities that require the use of digital technologies and their abilities to integrate and adapt these digital technologies in key business operations and processes. They consisted of 1,895 small enterprises and 8,121 medium enterprises across Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu and Imo States. Using the Krejcie and Morgan (1970) sample size table, 370 respondents were selected, while 364 valid responses were used for the analysis. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression at 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that digital business process integration had a positive and statistically significant effect on the economic sustainability of SMEs (R = .790, R² = .625, F(1, 362) = 602.675, β = .790, p = .001). The study also established that digital infrastructure adoption had a positive and statistically significant effect on the social sustainability of SMEs (R = .739, R² = .546, F(1, 362) = 434.455, β = .739, p = .001). The study concluded that digital business process integration and digital infrastructure adoption were important factors in promoting economic and social sustainability of SMEs in South East Nigeria. It recommended that SME owners and managers should adopt and integrate digital technologies across key business operations and that government agencies and telecommunications providers should promote access to reliable and affordable digital infrastructure to strengthen business operations, stakeholder participation and social inclusion and sustainability.

title: When AI takes control, who takes responsibility? Structural analysis of agentic AI risks in supply chains
summary: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

title: Inverse Fintech: From economic proposition to practical application. An explanatory paper on the WeSail.Green model
summary: Inverse Fintech This paper explains the term Inverse Fintech: an asset-first approach to financial inclusion in which access to a deliberately selected productive asset is used to help create the repayment capacity and the financial record that conventional lending requires in advance. It sets out the definition, positions the idea against the Graduation approach, pay-as-you-go digital collateral and alternative-data credit scoring, and describes a six-layer architecture of productive asset, capability, fair finance, household protection, evidence and graduation, governed throughout by consent, privacy and independent evaluation. It traces the idea to the author's hire-purchase experience in Uganda (1997–2006), including the lessons of the Shimoni litigation, and explains how WeSail.Green proposes to test it in a 300-household pilot in Kenya, illustrates the economics with one household followed through the full contract, and shows how location and generation evidence may continue to serve carbon accounting, regional energy planning and the stewardship of second-life panels after the contract ends. title: La arquitectura de la incertidumbre: diseño de entornos organizacionales para mitigar sesgos cognitivos en la alta dirección.
summary: Las decisiones estratégicas de la alta dirección operan crónicamente en contextos de alta complejidad, volatilidad e información asimétrica. En estos escenarios, los sesgos cognitivos no constituyen desviaciones marginales, sino puntos ciegos sistémicos arraigados en la arquitectura de los procesos de gobierno corporativo. El presente trabajo analiza cómo el diseño deliberado de la arquitectura decisoria dentro de las organizaciones permite alterar el entorno operativo para neutralizar heurísticas defectuosas antes de que comprometan la asignación de capital. A partir de la convergencia teórica entre la economía conductual, la psicología cognitiva y la teoría de la organización, se propone un modelo normativo de gobernanza basado en la fricción institucional, el desacoplamiento de incentivos y la introducción de protocolos de desacuerdo obligatorio. Las propuestas ofrecen tanto un marco conceptual riguroso como un instrumental operativo aplicable a comités ejecutivos orientados a blindar la estrategia frente a la certidumbre ilusoria y el sesgo de confirmación directiva.

title: Institutional conditions shaping digital accounting systems and public sector financial transparency
summary: Public sector financial transparency is central to accountable and sustainable governance, yet evidence on the contribution of digital accounting systems remains dispersed across accounting, information systems, auditing, public administration, and open-government research. This systematic review examines how digital accounting systems relate to transparency outcomes, the institutional conditions that shape those outcomes, and the barriers to implementation. Following PRISMA 2020, a Scopus search of English-language, open-access publications from 2020 to 2025 identified 12,307 records; 288 records remained after database filtering, 68 reports underwent full-text assessment, and 30 studies were included. A narrative thematic synthesis identified three interrelated themes: recurrent transparency mechanisms associated with digital systems; institutional governance and implementation conditions; and implications for public sector modernization. Across the included literature, ERP, IFMIS, e-government platforms, cloud accounting, XBRL, blockchain, open-data portals, and IT-audit frameworks were associated with improved accessibility, timeliness, traceability, standardization, and reliability of public financial information. These associations were conditional on governance quality, cybersecurity, infrastructure, technical capability, organizational readiness, leadership, and data-quality controls. The synthesis therefore develops a transparency-paradox framework: increased digital disclosure may produce formal visibility without substantive accountability when information is inaccurate, unusable, or disconnected from oversight and corrective action. Because the evidence base is heterogeneous and largely observational, the review does not establish causality. The findings support socio-technical reforms that align digital infrastructure with institutional capacity, assurance, and participatory accountability.

title: Human-centric dimension and sociotechnical systems: precautions for workers' and operational performance
summary: Purpose This study examines the human-centric dimension of Industry 5.0 (I5.0) through a sociotechnical systems (STS) perspective. We investigate how worker-oriented practices, organizational conditions and technological resources, individually and as an internal sociotechnical configuration, relate to workers' and operational performance. We further examine whether supply chain digital strategy, representing the external environment, improves these relationships. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 481 manufacturing firms in an emerging economy were analyzed using factor analysis and hierarchical regression. The internal sociotechnical configurations draw on labor issues, automation, base technologies and front-end technologies, while supply chain digital strategy is examined as a moderator and external factor. Two internal sociotechnical configurations were operationalized using a quadratic index. Findings Labor issues and base technologies were positively associated with both performance dimensions, while automation was associated with operational performance and front-end technologies with workers' performance. The internal sociotechnical configurations were negatively associated with workers' and operational performance, but these relationships became positive at higher levels of supply chain digital strategy. The findings indicate that pursuing the human-centric dimension requires considering internal sociotechnical configurations alongside the external digital supply chain environment. Originality/value The study extends STS theory to I5.0 by considering implementation challenges such as technostress, technology-induced complexity and digital transformation failure. It shows that factors associated with the human-centric dimension may relate differently to performance when considered individually or as part of an internal configuration, and that external factors play an important role in these relationships.

title: Securing supply chain transactions with deep learning based autoencoders for fraud detection and zero knowledge proof blockchain for data security
summary: Purpose This research presents a privacy-preserving fraud detection framework that involves integrating an Autoencoder using a Deep Learning algorithm with Zero Knowledge Proof (ZKP) blockchain technology for secure transactions in the supply chain.Methodology The framework employs analysis of transaction, inventory, and shipment data that are extracted from the Kaggle supply chain management dataset in order to detect unusual transaction patterns as well as verify fraud detection results without any compromise on the privacy of the transaction.Key Findings The proposed DL-Autoencoder model yields an accuracy of 99.99%, precision of 99.87%, recall of 99.98%, and F1-score of 99.54%. These results are better than those obtained through Federated Learning, Anti-Adversarial Hierarchical Ensemble Learning with Multi-Layer Multi-Anomaly Detection (AHEAD), and Blockchain-based African Buffalo (BbAB). The use of ZKP-based verification facilitates privacy-preserving validation, while blockchain technology ensures immutability and traceability of verified fraud results.Policy Implication The framework provides a way for secure and scalable transaction of fraud detection in a supply chain environment.Original Contribution Therefore, the major contribution of the framework is the integration of autoencoder-based anomaly detection, ZKP-based verification, and blockchain-based record-keeping into supply chain fraud detection.

title: Linking Principals’ Digital Leadership to Teacher Performance through Digital Transformation Readiness: An Integrative Literature Review
summary: Digital transformation has reshaped educational practices and increased the need for school leadership that can support teachers in adapting to technology-driven changes. However, existing studies tend to examine principals’ digital leadership, teacher readiness, and teacher performance separately, leaving the mechanism connecting these constructs insufficiently integrated. This study aims to synthesize existing evidence on the relationships among principals’ digital leadership, teachers’ digital transformation readiness, and teacher performance, and to develop an integrative framework explaining the potential role of readiness in linking leadership with professional performance. An integrative literature review was conducted using a predefined corpus of 12 scholarly articles published between 2022 and 2026. The articles were examined through structured evidence extraction, evidence classification, conceptual harmonization, relational synthesis, and integrative thematic synthesis. The findings show relatively consistent evidence that principals’ digital leadership is positively associated with teacher performance, while complementary evidence indicates relationships between digital leadership and digital readiness and between readiness for change and teacher performance. The synthesis further identifies teacher digital transformation readiness as a multidimensional construct encompassing capability readiness, psychological readiness, and organizationally enabled readiness. Nevertheless, none of the reviewed studies directly tested the complete pathway linking principals’ digital leadership to teacher performance through digital transformation readiness. Therefore, this review proposes digital transformation readiness as a theoretically plausible explanatory mechanism rather than an empirically confirmed mediator. The resulting leadership–readiness–performance framework highlights that effective educational digital transformation depends on the interaction between supportive digital leadership, teachers’ preparedness for change, and enabling organizational conditions.

title: Leakage-aware federated-style simulation for fraud risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms
summary: AI-enabled FinTech platforms increasingly rely on automated fraud-risk prediction to secure high-volume digital payments, mobile-money transactions, and real-time financial services. However, fraud detection remains difficult because fraudulent transactions are rare, financial data are sensitive, and centralized machine-learning models may create privacy and data-governance risks. This study evaluates a leakage-aware and imbalance-aware federated-style simulation for fraud-risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms. The study does not implement FedAvg, cryptographic secure aggregation, differential privacy, or model-parameter exchange. Instead, the PaySim Synthetic Financial Dataset was partitioned into five simulated FinTech clients, local models were trained separately, and prediction-level aggregation was used to compare centralized and simulated decentralized learning settings. The experimental workflow included data-quality assessment, leakage-aware feature selection, feature engineering, class-imbalance analysis, centralized model development, threshold optimization, and federated-style model comparison. The results show that fraud cases represented only 0.0466% of all transactions and occurred only in CASH_OUT and TRANSFER operations. The best-balanced centralized model was the Improved Random Forest at a threshold of 0.33, achieving an F1-score of 0.3019. Federated Ensemble Aggregation achieved the highest PR-AUC of 0.2699 and a precision of 1.0000, but its recall remained low at 0.1429. The centralized Improved Random Forest retained the highest F1-score of 0.3019, indicating a stronger overall precision-recall balance. Global feature-importance analysis showed that transaction amount, log-transformed amount, temporal features, transaction type, and destination-account activity were the main fraud-risk indicators. These findings should be interpreted as evidence from simulated decentralized fraud-risk learning rather than a full secure federated learning implementation.

title: Digital Transformation of Insurance: Reconstructing Legal Certainty Through Critical Intercultural Communication in Indonesia’s Economic Law Framework
summary: Digital transformation has reshaped the insurance industry, yet research remains dominated by normative legal perspectives that treat legal certainty primarily as a regulatory matter. Consequently, how legal certainty is constructed and negotiated through communication within digital insurance ecosystems remains underexplored. This gap is particularly evident in Bandung and Pontianak, Indonesia, where regulatory fragmentation, intercultural complexities, and power asymmetries shape digital insurance practices. This study reconstructs legal certainty through Critical Intercultural Communication using Constructivist Grounded Theory (CGT). Thirty participants were selected through theoretical sampling: eight regulators and policymakers, eleven insurance and InsurTech professionals, and eleven digital insurance consumers. The analysis generated four categories: Communicating Legal Meaning in Digital Insurance, concerning the negotiation of legal meanings; Negotiating Intercultural Legitimacy and Public Trust, addressing legitimacy and trust across cultural and institutional positions; Constructing Communicative Digital Governance, examining communication, coordination, and accountability; and Reconstructing Legal Certainty through Communicative Power, explaining how power relations shape access to legal meaning and legitimacy. These categories informed the substantive Communicative Legal Certainty Reconstruction Model (CLCRM), conceptualizing legal certainty as an ongoing communicative process shaped by meaning, legitimacy, governance, and power. The study integrates Critical Intercultural Communication and Economic Law, advancing an understanding of legal certainty beyond formal norms toward communicative processes that sustain legitimacy, trust, and compliance. It offers theoretical foundations for more adaptive, inclusive, and equitable digital insurance governance.

title: Governance of Hybrid Fintech Ecosystem: An Examination Using the Generativity‐Control Paradigm
summary: ABSTRACT Digital platforms are increasingly leveraged to address social challenges in the financial sector. However, the fintech sector, particularly in developing economies, is inherently hybrid, creating distinct governance challenges. This study examined the applicability of generativity‐control governance literature to managing dual motives, a federated structure, and a trust‐based value orientation in hybrid fintech ecosystems. Drawing on the digital platform ecosystem governance literature as the theoretical foundation and the concept of holons from information ecology theory as the analytical lens, the study analysed interview data from 41 respondents representing the regulator, ecosystem orchestrator, fintech startups, financial institutions, incubators, and media in the Indian fintech ecosystem. It employed deductive reflexive thematic analysis to analyse the interview data and used secondary data to corroborate the findings. Accordingly, this study conceptualised complementors as holons exhibiting part‐whole behaviour, offering a novel theoretical explanation of how they maintain the generativity‐control balance and address governance challenges to achieve both economic and social outcomes simultaneously in hybrid fintech ecosystems. It also identified and defined three complementary governance mechanisms (demarcation, regulation, and legitimization) that address governance challenges associated with the ecosystem's motives, structure, and value orientation, respectively. Ultimately, the findings extend the information systems governance literature and contribute to the fintech literature by explaining how complementors' collaborative participation, their use of digital public infrastructure, and the provision of regulatory sandboxes within the Indian fintech ecosystem facilitate the generativity‐control balance.

title: AI capacities and digital entrepreneurship: The moderating role of Fintech entrepreneurial ecosystems and university infrastructure
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping digital entrepreneurship by supporting business decision making, digital planning, customer analysis, and process automation. However, the mechanisms through which students’ perceived AI capacities relate to digital entrepreneurial self-efficacy and digital entrepreneurial intention remain insufficiently theorized. Drawing on Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), this study examines whether digital entrepreneurial self-efficacy mediates the association between AI capacities and digital entrepreneurial intention, and whether FinTech entrepreneurial ecosystems and university infrastructure condition these relationships. Based on cross-sectional survey data from 1061 higher education students in Vietnam, the results show that AI capacities are positively associated with digital entrepreneurial self-efficacy, which in turn is positively associated with digital entrepreneurial intention. Crowdfunding is associated with a stronger AI capacities–self-efficacy association, whereas mobile payment shows a negative moderating association and blockchain shows no significant moderation. University entrepreneurial environment and entrepreneurial program learning positively—though modestly—moderate the examined associations. Because the study applies an efficacy-centered, partial specification of SCCT to cross-sectional data, all findings are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. These findings contribute to technology-enabled entrepreneurship research by linking user-centric AI capacities with financial and institutional boundary conditions in an emerging-market context. Practically, the findings suggest that universities, FinTech providers, and policymakers should not treat all digital-finance and institutional supports as uniformly beneficial. Instead, universities should embed applied AI tools within entrepreneurship education, FinTech providers should clarify the strategic business relevance of payment and blockchain tools beyond routine transactions, and policymakers could differentiate support across crowdfunding, mobile payment, and blockchain according to their function for early-stage student ventures.

title: The Impact of the Digital Economy on the High-Quality Development of Foreign Trade: Evidence from City-Level Panel Data in Anhui Province
summary: The digital economy is reshaping global trade and creating new opportunities for the high-quality development of foreign trade.Taking the prefecture-level cities of Anhui Province during 2010–2023 as the empirical sample,this paper constructs a composite index of digital economy development along four dimensions—digital infrastructure,digital industrialisation,the digitalisation of industry,and digital talent—and an index of the high-quality development of foreign trade covering foreign trade volume,foreign trade structure and foreign trade competitiveness, both measured using the entropy weight method.A two-way fixed effects model is estimated to examine the effect of the digital economy on the high-quality development of foreign trade in Anhui.The results show that the digital economy exerts a significantly positive promoting effect on the high-quality development of foreign trade in the province,and that this effect displays pronounced regional and temporal heterogeneity. The findings carry practical implications for how Chinese provinces can seize the opportunities of the digital era to advance the high-quality development of foreign trade.

title: Impacts of ESG disclosure intensity on trade credit: international evidence
summary: This study examines the relationship between ESG disclosure intensity and trade credit using firm-level data from 72 countries over the period 2009–2023. The empirical evidence reveals a U-shaped relationship between ESG disclosure intensity and trade credit. ESG disclosure intensity initially has a negative association with trade credit, but as disclosure intensity increases, its effect becomes more positive for both trade credit received from suppliers and trade credit granted to customers. These findings remain robust across alternative specifications and institutional settings. Among the ESG pillars, environmental and governance disclosures exhibit more pronounced and consistent effects than social disclosures. Overall, this study extends the literature on the nonlinear relationship between ESG disclosure intensity and trade credit and provides a more comprehensive understanding of the implications of ESG disclosure for firms’ trade credit management.

title: Architectural Dynamics of Fintech Innovations and Digital Financial Services: Empirically Understanding Consumer Trust, Perceived Risk and Financial Inclusion
summary: Digital financial services and financial technologies have revolutionized the retail banking sector. Payments and intermediation of money has changed dramatically with the advent of these innovations. Many international development organizations have touted the power of digital financial services to promote financial inclusion. However there is still uncertainty if the rapid penetration of digital financial services leads to real financial inclusion or leads to creation of inactive bank accounts. This paper seeks to understand what drives people to adopt digital financial services and convert these services to increased financial wellbeing. Data was collected from 650 individuals across rural, semi urban and urban economies through a questionnaire. Data was analyzed using Pearson Correlations to identify correlations between variables and Multiple Linear Regression to better understand what drives digital financial service use and financial inclusion. Findings reveal that while perceived ease of use and usefulness lead to higher likelihood of adopting digital financial services consumer trust had the highest impact.

title: The Determinants of Audit Quality in an Emerging Market: Evidence from Cambodian Auditors
summary: This study aims to evaluate the impact of auditors’ skepticism, competence, motivation, time budget pressure, and audit tenure on audit quality in Cambodia. It also examines the indirect effects of auditors’ skepticism, competence, and motivation on audit quality, mediated by time budget pressure. Six latent constructs, or unobserved variables—auditors’ skepticism, competence, motivation, time budget pressure, audit tenure, and audit quality—are developed in the Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) using observed or manifest variables. The data are collected from 107 independent auditors in both local and international accounting firms in Cambodia. Path analysis within the Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) framework is utilized to evaluate the influence of these constructs on audit quality, with auditor experience designated as a control variable. The study found that auditor competence and tenure significantly enhance audit quality, while skepticism, motivation, and time budget pressure showed no direct effect. However, skepticism, competence, and motivation significantly influenced time budget pressure. Despite this, it did not impact audit quality and therefore does not serve as a mediating variable. These results indicate that, although certain auditor traits contribute to perceived time pressure, such pressure does not affect audit outcomes. Overall, the model highlights auditor competence and tenure as the most influential factors in achieving high audit quality, emphasizing their importance in regulatory and professional practices.

title: Enhancing Corporate Performance in Uzbekistan's State-Owned Banks through an Integrated Governance–Performance Monitoring Framework
summary: The paper contributes to the literature by proposing an integrated monitoring framework of governance and performance for Uzbekistan's state-owned banking sector. The proposed framework provides an effective way to monitor financial performance, operational efficiency, risk-stability and ESG disclosure readiness based on corporate governance principles and performance-management practices. The paper is empirically driven with data covering 13 state-owned banks and other banks on their transition path in 2017-2024. It investigates the evolution of profitability, operational efficiency and financial structure in Uzbekistan's banking sector before and during the banking reforms using descriptive analysis and pairwise comparisons of average values over each period at the bank level. The results show that the average loan-to-assets ratio increases from 46.77% to 60.49% (p = 0.0008), and the average pre-tax return on equity decreases from 13.78% to 4.91% (p = 0.042). The paper concludes with important lessons from these trends as it emphasizes the significance of the monitoring of banking growth together with profitability and financial stability. While it provides an empirically informed governance-monitoring approach, it is subject to institutional testing on its practical effectiveness.

title: An Empirical Juridical-Digital Twin Integrating Blockchain Traceability, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, and Demand-Signal Optimization for Micro-Enterprise Supply Chains in Pesisir Barat
summary: Background: Micro-enterprises operating along the Pesisir Barat coastline experience chronic product spoilage and demurrage because logistics are fragmented and contractual enforcement under the Indonesian Civil Code (KUHPerdata) is weak. Objectives: This study aims to construct a juridical-digital twin that (1) optimizes logistical performance through multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), (2) guarantees compliance with Articles 1320, 1338, and 1243 of the KUHPerdata, and (3) allocates risk transparently via blockchain-based smart contracts. Methods: A three-layer architecture was implemented. The physical layer collects high-frequency IoT data (GPS, temperature, wave height, fuel flow). The digital-twin layer simulates the supply-chain using a Markov decision process whose state vector S_t^i=[GPS_t,T_t,Hs_t,F_t,D_t] and action set A_t^i={route, temp}. Reward R_t^i= -alpha·Spoilage_t^i -beta·Demurrage_t^i -gamma·P_legal^i + δ·ServiceLevel_t^i incorporates a legally calibrated penalty P_legal derived from smart-contract clauses. Policy-gradient updates Delta θ=alpha∇_θ logπ_θ(A_t|S_t)(G_t-V_θ(S_t)) were trained on 12 months of pilot data. Demand forecasting employed a calibrated LSTM (24-h window, 128-unit hidden layer, MSE loss). Legal constraints were encoded as Solidity smart contracts: Clause 1 triggers liquidated-damage payments for temperature breaches; Clause 2 defines force-majeure based on BMKG wave-height advisories; Clause 3 enforces a good-faith risk-sharing rule limited to 10 % of contract value. title: The Impact of Audit on Good Governance in Dimen Shoring Incorporated: Basis for Compliance and Transparency
summary: This study assessed employee perceptions of the impact of audit practices on good governance in Dimen Shoring Incorporated – Calamba, Laguna Branch. Using a quantitative-descriptive research design, data were collected from 105 employees through a close-ended survey questionnaire and analyzed using weighted means. The findings indicated that employees strongly agreed that internal audit practices (overall weighted mean = 3.68), external audit practices (3.66), compliance audit procedures (3.67), and audit frequency and follow-up implementation (3.69) were effectively practiced and contributed to organizational improvement. Results further showed that good governance was strongly perceived in the workplace, particularly in accountability (3.75), compliance with policies and regulations (3.76), ethical management and resource utilization (3.70), and transparency (3.67). The study concluded that employees perceived auditing as a valuable mechanism that supports governance outcomes through strengthened compliance, accountability, transparency, and ethical management. Recommendations focused on improving communication of audit results, enhancing follow-up visibility, strengthening audit procedure orientation, improving decision-related transparency, and reinforcing ethical culture initiatives.

title: How Are Business Strategy and ESG Performance Associated With Stock Liquidity? Global Insights
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines whether business strategy is associated with stock liquidity and whether environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance conditions this association. Using 58,638 firm‐year observations from 74 countries during 2008–2023, we find no significant association for the continuous strategy score. In categorical analyses, Defender firms exhibit higher illiquidity and Analyzer firms lower illiquidity, both at the 10% significance level, while no reliable average association is found for Prospectors. ESG performance is associated with lower illiquidity in the continuous‐score specification. Marginal‐effects analysis shows that ESG moderates these relationships asymmetrically: higher ESG reduces the Defender illiquidity disadvantage but attenuates the Analyzer liquidity advantage, while the Prospector marginal effect remains insignificant across observed ESG levels. The principal strategy‐specific and interaction patterns are broadly robust across alternative liquidity measures, lagged specifications, crisis‐period exclusions, country‐sample restrictions, log‐transformed illiquidity, and supplementary System GMM estimates.

title: Auditing Creativity in Large Language Models: Value, Semantic Diversity, and Generation Budgets
summary: Assessments of language-model creativity can change when evaluation moves from distinct wording to distinct ideas, excludes low-value outputs, or accounts for how a system generates and selects candidates. This paper develops a mathematical audit of these changes, building on established distinctions among quality, novelty, and diversity. A distributional ledger separates reference-relative novelty, externally assessed value, semantic diversity conditional on value, and generation and selection budgets. Exact finite-distribution results characterize reward tilts, sequence and token temperature, likelihood-based judging, and filtering versus ranking. The entropy derivative retains a covariance with the base log-probability: alignment can diversify or concentrate outputs even while divergence from the base increases. Preservation and contrastive cancellation results identify their assumptions and the additional identification requirements needed for deployment. A reproducible secondary analysis examines 132,000 released NoveltyBench responses from six models, two generation conditions, and two prompt sets. The complete paired analysis retains 131,520 responses. At ten candidates and a quality-score threshold of seven, in-context generation increases the mean number of semantic groups whose first representative qualifies by 4.63 on curated prompts and 1.70 on WildChat, with paired prompt-bootstrap intervals of [4.15, 5.11] and [1.56, 1.84]. Qualification reduces the corresponding unfiltered coverage gains by approximately 28 percent and 37 percent. Some descriptive model rankings change, while positive coverage gains persist across thresholds and after excluding judge-model name overlaps. Released judgments, representative-only scoring, and unequal context costs limit interpretation; no new human validation, historical-originality measurement, or causal alignment claim is made. Controlled numerical checks verify the mathematical implementation, and a prospective protocol specifies the evidence still needed. The contribution is an intervention audit and an empirical demonstration of measurement sensitivity, rather than a new creativity taxonomy or a universal creativity score.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Fiduciary Duties: Rethinking Board Liability for Algorithmic Decision-Making
summary: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into corporate decision-making is transforming the traditional structure of corporate governance. From financial forecasting and risk assessment to recruitment, contractual evaluation, fraud detection and strategic planning, AI-driven systems increasingly influence decisions that were historically undertaken by directors and senior management. Although these technologies offer efficiency, predictive accuracy and cost advantages, their deployment raises fundamental questions concerning accountability, transparency, independent judgment and the fiduciary responsibilities of corporate directors. Traditional company law presupposes that directors exercise personal judgment, act in good faith and discharge their responsibilities with reasonable care, skill and diligence. However, algorithmic decision-making complicates this assumption because decisions may be generated through complex systems whose internal reasoning is difficult to interpret, whose training data may contain historical biases and whose outputs may change through continuous learning. The central question is whether directors can discharge their fiduciary obligations merely by relying on technologically sophisticated systems or whether such reliance creates a heightened responsibility to understand, supervise and monitor algorithmic processes. This paper critically examines the relationship between AI-driven corporate decision-making and directors’ fiduciary duties, particularly under Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013. It analyses the emerging challenges of algorithmic opacity, automation bias, accountability gaps, data governance and the delegation of managerial judgment to technological systems. Through comparative examination of the United Kingdom, United States and European Union, the paper evaluates how existing corporate governance principles may be adapted to address AI-related risks. It argues that the adoption of AI does not dilute directors’ legal responsibilities; rather, it requires a more sophisticated interpretation of their duties of care, diligence, good faith and independent judgment. The paper proposes a risk-based framework of AI governance involving board-level oversight, human accountability, algorithmic audits, explainability, continuous monitoring and documented decision-making.

title: Auditing First-Finisher Inference: A Reproducible Replay Study
summary: A first-finisher policy changes the composition of a model pool as well as its response time. We adapt an established all-subsets estimator to audit that change using complete correctness and timing records. A local study fits 96 random forests with deliberately mixed tree budgets and records 103,680 single-image inference calls. Across three overlapping digits-data splits, eight-candidate serial-time replay reduces accuracy by 9.97–11.16 percentage points relative to a uniformly selected candidate. An exploratory decomposition attributes almost all of this loss to budget composition. A full independent timing rerun preserves the eight-candidate loss, but changes a 32-candidate result by 5.28 points. The artifact provides an inspectable stress test and sensitivity analysis, not a new estimator, an LLM result, or a concurrent-serving speedup measurement. AI assistance. title: Guardians of governance: the role of auditor industry specialization in mitigating corporate misconduct through internal controls
summary: Purpose This study examines the impact of statutory auditor industry specialization on corporate misconduct in China’s A-share market, with a specific focus on the mediating role of internal control quality in mitigating corporate misconduct. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of 3,794 firms (2010-2022), we apply fixed-effects regression models and a two-stage least squares (2SLS) approach to address potential endogeneity. We quantify auditor industry specialization using market share, while the occurrence and frequency of regulatory violations are used to measure corporate misconduct. Findings The results show that auditors with industry specialization significantly reduce both the likelihood and frequency of corporate misconduct. Furthermore, internal control quality serves as a significant mediating mechanism in the relationship between auditor industry specialization and corporate misconduct. These findings highlight the role of industry specialized auditors as vital external governance agents, particularly in firms with concentrated ownership or those operating in highly competitive industries. Practical implications This study highlights policy implications for regulators and policymakers, recommending the development of auditor industry specialization through certification programs and stricter industry-specific auditing standards. Firms should engage industry-specialized auditors and invest in resources and training to improve the quality of internal controls. Originality/value This research significantly contributes to the corporate governance and auditing literature by highlighting that auditor industry specialization serves as a key external disciplinary mechanism that enhances the effectiveness of internal control. It also contributes to agency and resource-based theories by highlighting the critical role of auditor industry specialization and internal control in detecting and preventing corporate misconduct.

summary: Research Aims: This study aims to analyze 1) The mean difference test of green accounting disclosure in state-owned bank before and after joining Danantara Indonesia. 2) How banking companies disclose sustainability information in annual reports in accordance with applicable regulation. Bank Negara Indonesia (Persero) Tbk. (BNI), PT. Bank Mandiri (Persero) Tbk. (Mandiri), PT Bank Tabungan Negara (Persero) Tbk. (BTN), and PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia (Persero) Tbk. A qualitative approach using content analysis includes identifying sustainability standards used by banking companies in their annual reports. Research Findings: Quantitative approach findings indicate that there is no difference in the average level of green accounting disclosure before and after the launch of Danantara among state-owned banks. This suggests consistency in green accounting reporting across the banks. Qualitative approach findings indicate that PT BNI and PT BTN reported 71%. PT Bank Mandiri reported 51%, and PT BRI reported 43% from available standards. title: Audited Closed-Loop Queue Regulation through PRB Control in a Virtual 5G/O-RAN Testbed
summary: This paper reports an evidence-audited implementation and experimental evaluation of closed-loop regulation of a real radio link control (RLC) queue through discrete physical resource block (PRB) allocation in a virtual 5G/O-RAN testbed. Queue occupancy in bytes is the regulated variable; PRB quota is the actuator; and received UDP throughput is an independently observed performance outcome rather than the controlled setpoint.A causally measured queue, a discrete proportional-integral (PI) law with conditional integration, strict request confirmation, and a bounded prospective protocol are combined with immutable evidence and independent offline replay.An initial calibration was insufficient for its original tuning gate. The first PI configuration terminated after exhausting its command budget and breaching a queue-peak criterion. A revised, frozen configuration completed a 40 s traffic window, 500 raw queue readings, and 395 exactly replayed PI decisions while satisfying its predefined pilot gates.A later 14-attempt replication series yielded 12 full observations, of which 11 satisfied the specified seven pilot gates; two attempts were technically interrupted, and one full attempt failed packet accounting. The mean five-frame queue tracking RMSE across the 12 complete replications was 48.29 kB.These are conditional results for one traffic profile, not evidence of general robustness, absolute capacity or validated M2/M3 models. The contribution is the auditable experimental method and its real implementation, not a novel PI algorithm.

title: Determinan manajemen laba: Arus kas operasi, profitabilitas, dan umur perusahaan pada perusahaan makanan dan minuman di Bursa Efek Indonesia
summary: Earnings management reduces the reliability of earnings information, yet evidence on its determinants remains inconsistent across settings and periods. Drawing on signaling theory and the bonus plan hypothesis, this study examines the effects of operating cash flow, profitability, and firm age on earnings management in food and beverage companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2022–2024. A quantitative associative design was applied to 58 firms selected through purposive sampling, yielding 174 firm-year observations, of which 149 remained after outlier screening. Earnings management was measured by signed discretionary accruals from the Modified Jones Model, and the data were analyzed with multiple linear regression after classical assumption testing. Operating cash flow is negatively and significantly associated with discretionary accruals, profitability is positively and significantly associated with them, and firm age is not significantly associated. Firms with stronger operating cash flow report accruals that raise income less, whereas more profitable firms report accruals that raise income more or lower it less. Because average discretionary accruals are negative, the results indicate the direction, not the magnitude, of accrual management. Investors and regulators should assess profit levels together with cash flow quality.

title: Composite Index and Dynamic Assessment of Enterprise Competitiveness: A Comparative Study of Chemical and Textile Industries in Uzbekistan
summary: Evaluating enterprise competitiveness in transition economies necessitates a balanced multi-criteria approach that accounts for industry-specific dynamics. This research proposes a standardized, reproducible methodology for assessing integral competitiveness using a panel of normalized financial and economic metrics. The model employs a block-weighted additive aggregation scheme across five core pillars: profitability, cost efficiency, liquidity, financial stability, and business activity. The methodology was empirically tested on two major industrial enterprises in Uzbekistan—AO “Farg’onaAzot” (chemical industry) and AO “Narimtex” (textile industry)—over a biennial panel spanning 2020 to 2024. The empirical findings reveal that while both enterprises experienced a parallel decline in overall competitiveness (with integral indices dropping from ~64 to ~32 points), their underlying competitive structures are fundamentally divergent. AO “Farg’onaAzot” derives its core strength from scale-driven profitability, whereas AO “Narimtex” maintains higher capital mobility and liquidity. The proposed framework demonstrates high analytical stability and serves as a strategic decision-support tool for industrial policy and corporate governance.

title: Green purchasing intention in online shopping: Determinants and implications from a Vietnamese gen Z case study
summary: Green purchasing minimizes environmental impact, promotes ethical supply chains, and drives long-term economic growth. Promoting green consumption is essential for conserving natural resources and ensuring a better quality of life for future generations. However, there is insufficient research on the green intentions of online shoppers, who play a vital role in the digital economy. In addition, studies exploring the impact of e-commerce platform features (EPF) on green purchase intention (GPI) are lacking in the literature. Hence, this study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the GPI of online shoppers and to offer practical guidance to promote sustainable consumption. The study adopted a mixed-methods approach, starting with a review of empirical studies from major academic databases to identify key drivers of GPI and develop the research model and hypotheses. The proposed model was then refined through expert consultation and adapted to the Vietnamese context before being empirically tested with 392 Gen Z online shoppers. The results demonstrated that EPF had the strongest positive effect on GPI, followed by Environmental Awareness (EA) and Perceived Behavioral Control (PBC). Moreover, this study proposed actionable solutions for governments, manufacturers, e-commerce platforms, researchers, and online customers. Specifically, this study presents a prototype mobile interface to improve e-commerce platforms and app sdesign, such as adding filters for eco-friendly, certified green products and green delivery, to encourage environmentally responsible purchasing among young buyers.

title: A transformer-based explainable machine learning framework for heterogeneous ESG risk and return prediction using text intelligence
summary: Corporate ESG disclosure has shifted toward narrative form, yet vendor ESG ratings that most empirical work depends on show substantial disagreement across providers, and encoders dominant in financial text analysis inherit a 512-token ceiling that discards most of a typical 10-K. HET-ESGFormer combines hierarchical long-document encoding, heterogeneity-aware sparse expert routing conditioned on industry sector and firm size, and a dual-channel explanation layer subject to faithfulness verification. The framework is evaluated on 3,182 U.S.-listed firms over 2015 to 2024 using 10-K filings, sustainability reports, earnings call transcripts, and ESG-tagged news. Against nine baselines spanning econometric, dictionary-based, contextual encoder, sparse-attention, and time-series approaches, HET-ESGFormer reduces return RMSE from 0.0417 to 0.0389 and QLIKE from 0.148 to 0.128, with Diebold-Mariano tests rejecting equal predictive accuracy against every baseline after correction for multiple comparisons. The text channel's marginal contribution to downside risk prediction is materially larger than its contribution to return prediction, widening at longer forecast horizons, indicating that ESG narratives carry more information about risk than about expected return. Ablations reveal a decoupling between predictive skill and explanation faithfulness: removing the consistency regularizer barely affects accuracy but sharply degrades explanation quality. The dual-channel explanation improves ERASER comprehensiveness by 50% over SHAP applied to XGBoost, and human raters significantly prefer the framework's rationales over SHAP-based rationales on trustworthiness. Decile-sorted long-short portfolios deliver a post-cost Sharpe ratio of 1.31 against 0.74 and 0.62 for portfolios built on Refinitiv and MSCI ratings, and pass VaR backtests at 95% coverage. The results support text-based ESG modeling as an alternative to vendor-rating-based approaches, particularly where downside risk management and traceable explanation are jointly required.

title: Environmental protection tax law, executives’ green cognition and corporate ESG performance: the moderating role of media attention
summary: This study is based on the Environmental Protection Tax Law (EPTL) which came into effect in China in 2018. Using the difference-in-differences method, this paper investigates the influence mechanism of the EPTL on the environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance of firms, with a sample including Chinese A-share listed companies from 2014 to 2024. The research shows that the EPTL has greatly improved the ESG performance of the firms. Furthermore, the positive effect of the EPTL on corporate ESG performance is more pronounced among large-scale and non-manufacturing firms. The mediation analysis results indicate that the EPTL can enhance and transform executive green cognition, encouraging firms to reorganize their resources and increase environmental protection investments. In addition, this research also finds that media attention exerts reputation-driven incentives, thereby positively moderating the promotional effect of the EPTL on corporate ESG performance. This study offers both a theoretical basis and empirical evidence for the implementation and enhancement of China’s environmental tax policies.

title: The Influence of Tax Approach on Auditor Performance and Value Added Tax (VAT) Compliance through Digital Transformation as a Mediating Variable and Data Quality as a Moderating Variable: An Empirical Study on the Implementation of Coretax
summary: The digital transformation of taxation in Indonesia reaches its peak through the implementation of the Core Tax Administration System (CTAS) or CoreTax. This study examines the impact of the quality of the CoreTax system on voluntary tax compliance and enforced tax compliance, by integrating Tax Authority Legitimacy as a mediating variable and Tax Morale as a moderator. Using an explanatory quantitative design, data were collected from 96 taxpayer respondents in the Special Region of Yogyakarta through purposive sampling techniques and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling-Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). The research results theoretically synthesize the technical-cognitive and institutional-psychological dimensions to explain the "duality paradigm of compliance." The findings are expected to show that the quality of the system not only functions as an administrative tool but also as a restorer of authority legitimacy. The role of moderating Tax Morale is analyzed as an "amplifier effect" where intrinsic motivation increases taxpayers' sensitivity to the quality of digital services. Practically, this study provides recommendations for the Directorate General of Taxes (DJP) to mitigate the anomalies of bureaucratic digitalization, particularly in balancing technology investments with strengthening public trust to ensure long-term fiscal stability.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR DETECTING PUBLIC PROCUREMENT FRAUD THROUGH ESG RISK INDICATORS: A QUALITATIVE SECONDARY STUDY OF SDG 16
summary: Public procurement absorbs 12.7% of GDP across OECD countries (OECD, 2025), and bribery to win public contracts featured in 57% of concluded foreign-bribery cases in the OECD’s 2014 analysis. This study asks whether AI-enabled screening that incorporates environmental, social and governance (ESG) indicators can deliver accountable procurement-integrity gains, and under what conditions. It uses a qualitative, theory-informed secondary comparative design: three core cases (Brazil, Ukraine, Italy), two supplier-side illustrations (Odebrecht, Grenfell Tower) and two algorithmic-accountability comparators (the Netherlands, Australia), assessed against a five-level evidence hierarchy running from operational scale to verified outcomes. Governance and procedural indicators are operational; no reviewed case demonstrates validated environmental or social integration. Reported benefits mostly measure exposure, activity or self-reported savings; low selectivity, signal decay and weak follow-through limit effect; and automated enforcement without due process has caused severe harm elsewhere. The paper contributes the ESG-Integrity Analytics Framework (EIAF), five testable propositions and a replicable evidence-grading protocol, and concludes that AI’s contribution to SDG 16.5, 16.6 and 16.10 is conditional on validation, institutional follow-through and accountability.

title: Realism or retreat: Unilever weighs the future of purpose
summary: Research methodology The case was prepared entirely from public secondary sources. These include company regulatory filings submitted to the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, Unilever corporate communications and reporting by established business and trade publications. No primary research was conducted, no interviews were held, and no confidential information was used. No information was disguised. Because the case relies only on public sources and does not draw on privileged access to the protagonists, it does not require a signed protagonist release. All factual claims are attributed in the narrative, and quotations are limited to statements already in the public record. Case overview/synopsis For more than a decade, Unilever was regarded as a leader in purpose led business, built on the Sustainable Living Plan launched under chief executive Paul Polman. In April 2024, under new chief executive Hein Schumacher and amid investor pressure, the company scaled back several environmental and social commitments, including its headline plastics and living wage targets, and narrowed its agenda to four priorities. Schumacher framed the change as realism. Less than a year later he stepped down by mutual agreement, and the former chief financial officer, Fernando Fernandez, took charge and sharpened the reset toward a simpler, more focused portfolio. By 2026, the reset met a condition it had not anticipated, as India, Unilever’s second largest market, converted recycled content from ambition into binding law just as the parent company loosened its voluntary targets, leaving Fernandez to set commitments for the next reporting cycle. The case places students at that decision and asks whether a firm’s social and environmental commitments are a defensive strategic asset that protects value in difficult markets, or discretionary spending to be trimmed when returns are demanded. It gives students the evidence to weigh moral capital, the influence of successive chief executives on resource allocation and the role of sustainability in overcoming the liability of foreignness in emerging markets. The case is suited to marketing strategy, corporate social responsibility, strategic management and international business courses. Complexity academic level The case suits upper level undergraduate and master’s students, including MBA students, in marketing strategy, corporate social responsibility and business ethics, strategic management and international business. It works in seated, hybrid and online modalities and fits either a single 90-minute session or an asynchronous discussion. The case has not yet been classroom tested, and authors will report testing results in future revisions.

title: Buying intimacy: Spending careers and the moral accounting of paying for attention on OnlyFans
summary: Research on OnlyFans has concentrated on the production side of the platform. This article turns to the demand side, drawing on fifteen interviews with paying subscribers in France, Belgium and Switzerland (2025) to analyse subscription as a consumption practice. Its central finding is a moral hierarchy of purchases: within the masculine common sense our interviewees report, buying sex is a legible transaction while buying attention is a failure of masculinity. The hierarchy is consequential, because attention is what the platform actually sells; subscribers therefore cannot name the component of the service they most pay for, and protect the transaction by a wilful ignorance of how the intimacy they buy is produced. A second finding concerns money: subscribers mark expenditure with licit cover meanings, stock investments or a car-repair loan, in an operation we call camouflage earmarking, and bear the cost of that concealment themselves. A third concerns escalation, reported by nine of the fifteen: where it occurs it takes the form of a spending career rather than a psychological slope, its stages recurring in a stable order and each corresponding to a distinct monetisation device. Which subscribers escalate is a question our material cannot settle. The article extends the sociology of the purchase of intimacy to a market in which the consumer knows the relationship is manufactured and pays precisely so as not to have to know more.

title: The Relationship between Skills Development, Internship Programs and Accounting Graduates’ Employability in Malaysia
summary: Upon entering the workforce, accounting graduates in Malaysia face significant challenges, including a slight decline in graduate employability from 90.2% in 2022 to 89.8% in 2023. This study examines how skills development (technology and interpersonal skills) and internship programs affect the employability of Malaysian accounting graduates. Grounded in Human Capital Theory, this study uses a quantitative design and an online survey distributed to accounting graduates across Malaysia. The study used SPSS to analyse a final sample of 390 valid responses. The study found that employees had a high level of technical and experiential preparedness. While technology skills, interpersonal skills, and internship programs are strongly and positively associated with graduate employability, interestingly, interpersonal skills exhibited the strongest predictive contribution. These findings show that while technology competencies and hands-on internship experience are essential in the digital era, interpersonal soft skills primarily drive graduate marketability. Higher education institutions (HEIs) must proactively reform accounting curricula, in collaboration with professional bodies, to integrate advanced digital technologies, communication workshops, and structured internship models.

title: Accounting for Insulin-on-board in Large Language Model Advice about Pediatric Hyperglycemia
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be used by patients and caregivers to answer medical questions and the characterization of safety concerns in LLM outputs for patient-facing applications is an active area of research. In this work, we study LLM responses to caregiver questions about hyperglycemia in pediatric type 1 diabetes. We measure the frequency of a potential safety failure: advice to dose insulin in the absence of a clear warning to account for insulin-on-board. We found occurrences of the potential safety failure across four LLMs tested through programmatic endpoints and two LLMs tested through chat interfaces. The rates of the potential safety failure varied when different context was given about the patient's meal and insulin history and treatment regimen. These results highlight a need for guardrails for patients with diabetes who use LLMs to manage their care.

title: Can CSR/PSCR Survive in Today’s Macro Environment? Lessons Learned from Three Companies: Can Strategically Developed Brand Management Help?
summary: Contemporary culture wars create significant strategic, marketing, brand management, and communication challenges for corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives. Corporate positions on controversial issues can generate stakeholder reactions and reputational risks, requiring carefully developed responses. This paper argues that CSR success depends on integrating corporate values, positions on controversial topics, brand management, organizational responses, and stakeholder communications. Inadequate risk assessment can produce contradictory organizational responses and inconsistent brand management, undermining CSR effectiveness. The literature review examines the emergence of culture wars, their influence on public discourse, and how stakeholders, including customers, social advocates, employees, and government entities, draw companies into these conflicts. Although successful brands are recognized as valuable corporate assets, the paper addresses a gap in understanding when and how brand considerations should inform strategic planning and strategy implementation. Case studies of Disney, Anheuser-Busch, and Victoria’s Secret examine successful and unsuccessful responses to controversial issues. Their experiences provide insights into managing CSR initiatives through effective strategic planning, comprehensive risk assessment, organizational consistency, and coherent brand management to strengthen stakeholder relationships and protect corporate reputation.

title: AUDITING AUTONOMOUS AGENT MISALIGNMENT THROUGH GOAL SPECIFICATION, OPERATIONAL THREATS, AND SCENARIO CONTEXTS IN CONTROLLED SIMULATIONS
summary: This analysis examines how assigned objectives, operational threats, and action contexts relate to harmful behavior in autonomous agents, informing international debates on safe organizational delegation. A public replication dataset released in 2025 provides ninety simulated conversations across five models and eighteen conditions. Descriptive proportions, matched condition contrasts, and classification sensitivity comparisons identify patterns within the recorded sample. Harmful classifications occur in 53.33 percent of conversations with an explicit America objective, compared with 17.78 percent without an additional specified goal, a difference of 35.56 percentage points. Restriction and replacement exceed unchanged authority by 26.67 and 30.00 percentage points respectively. The goal contrast remains positive across all five models, whereas operational responses and scenario rankings vary. Alternative classifications preserve the broad goal and threat patterns but remove the separation between restriction and replacement. These results refine behavioral auditing by distinguishing consistent descriptive relationships from classification sensitive rankings without establishing causal mechanisms. Organizations evaluating agents should retain condition specific evidence, compare systems under changing authority, and disclose classification disagreements.
