title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Governance in Procurement: Skills Transformation, Decision-Making Accountability and Ethical Issues
summary: This article analyzes the impact of generative artificial intelligence on the procurement function, starting from two converging directions: the operational and strategic transformation of procurement through GenAI, and the ethical issues generated by its use in processes involving suppliers, commercial data, contracts, and decisions with economic or legal effects. The paper proposes an integrated analytical framework in which GenAI is examined simultaneously as an efficiency-enhancing technology, a cognitive augmentation tool, and a source of organizational risk. The study adopts an empirical qualitative design based on an open-ended questionnaire completed by 40 professionals from procurement, IT, legal, compliance, and retail/supply chain, analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. The findings show that GenAI is valued mainly for preparatory, document-intensive tasks, while respondents reject its use for autonomous decisions with legal or economic effects; confidentiality, hallucinations, and diffuse accountability emerge as the dominant concerns. Building on these findings, the paper proposes a risk-tiered governance matrix that links GenAI use cases to control mechanisms and professional competences. The results indicate that the responsible adoption of GenAI depends less on the isolated technical performance of tools and more on the existence of an institutional architecture combining data quality, human oversight, auditability, protection of confidential information, and continuous professional training. The main conclusion is that the future of GenAI-assisted procurement should not be built on replacing the human decision-maker, but on controlled human–AI collaboration, in which generative systems support analysis while decision-making responsibility remains clearly allocated to the organization and its professionals.

title: Protocol OMEGA-T: QKD-Structured Secure Dissemination Doctrine and Polycrisis Engagement Architecture for Legacy Automotive Governance, Hydrogen Asset Misvaluation, and Climate Lobbying Accountability
summary: This monograph establishes the final execution doctrine and cryptographic dissemination architecture for Protocol "OMEGA-T," an institutional accountability and market-rectification framework targeting structural governance failures, capital misallocation, and obstructive climate lobbying within legacy automotive conglomerates (specifically examining Toyota Motor Corporation and the Toyota Industries buyout valuation dispute). Adopting Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) as both an operational security (OpSec) standard and an information-theoretic doctrine of Perfect Forward Secrecy and source unobservability, this study models how high-integrity evidentiary payloads are routed to high-resonance institutional actors to induce a deterministic polycrisis.The analytical architecture is structured across three strategic quadrants: 1. Media Intelligence (The NYT Triumvirate): Contextual payload tailoring for investigative journalism across technological fraud and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicle (FCV/Mirai) infrastructure collapse (John Carreyrou), systemic climate policy obstruction and InfluenceMap lobbying forensics (Hiroko Tabuchi), and industrial strategy failure amidst global battery electric vehicle (BEV) dominance (Jack Ewing). 2. Capital Market Enforcement (Activist & Institutional Stewardship): Leveraging internal valuation discrepancies, cross-shareholding conflicts of interest, and board independence deficits in the Toyota Industries privatization bid to empower activist intervention (Elliott Investment Management), active asset owners (Hosking Partners), ESG pension funds, and proxy advisors (ISS, Glass Lewis) under fiduciary duty and Caremark oversight standards. 3. Civil Society & Regulatory Accountability: Synchronizing empirical lobbying disclosures with NGO scorecards (InfluenceMap, Lead the Charge, Public Citizen, Sierra Club) to quantify the social and environmental costs of regulatory delay. Finally, the monograph specifies a zero-footprint cryptographic logistics sequence utilizing Tails OS, Tor-routed SecureDrop onion endpoints, MAT2 metadata sanitization, and linguistic stylometry flattening, ensuring mathematically verifiable payload authenticity alongside absolute source anonymity.

title: AI-Focused Promotional Positioning and Client Attribution of Responsibility for Accounting Firm Service Failures
summary: Accounting firms are investing heavily in generative AI and increasingly promoting these investments as central to their service models. While such messaging signals innovation and efficiency, it may also influence how clients assign blame when service errors occur. Drawing on attribution theory, this study employs a between-subjects experimental design to test whether clients assign responsibility for errors differently based on a firm’s marketing emphasis on generative AI versus traditional services. Participants read a scenario in which a firm-prepared tax return contained errors. In one condition, the accounting firm’s marketing highlighted its use of generative AI tools; in the other, it emphasized a focus on traditional services. The source of the error was left ambiguous. Participants exposed to AI-promoting messaging attributed more blame for the errors to the firm, perceived it as having greater control over error prevention, and judged the errors as more likely to recur. These findings suggest that promoting generative AI in firm marketing may raise client expectations about control and reliability, increasing reputational risk even when the technology’s role in an error is unclear. The study contributes to research on attribution in professional services and highlights a potential tradeoff: firms that emphasize technological sophistication may also be seen as more culpable when things go wrong.

title: Human Resource Accounting Information and Investment Evaluation: Evidence from Individual Retail Investors in Karnataka
summary: Human Resource Accounting Information (HRAI) gives details about an organisation’s human resources and can provide investors with additional information for evaluating investment opportunities. However, its effective use is influenced by investors’ level of knowledge, their perception of its relevance and the ease with which the information can be accessed, understood and evaluated. The present study examines the knowledge, perceived usefulness and hindrances associated with HRAI among NSE-registered individual retail investors in Karnataka. A quantitative descriptive research design was adopted, and data were collected from 287 individual retail investors using a structured questionnaire administered through both online and offline modes. The HRAI items were classified into five dimensions through Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), namely HR Valuation, HR Composition, HR Performance, Employee Benefits and Employee Governance. The responses were analysed using descriptive statistics and one-sample t-tests. The results indicate that investors have a low level of knowledge across all five dimensions, with the mean scores of the individual knowledge items falling below the scale average. In contrast, respondents expressed a high level of perceived usefulness of HRAI for investment evaluation, with mean scores ranging from 4.33 to 4.41. HRAI was particularly perceived as useful for comparing companies, assessing investment in human resources and their contribution to company performance, and evaluating investment opportunities. The findings also reveal substantial hindrances in accessing and evaluating HRAI, with mean scores ranging from 4.35 to 4.51. Information overload, inconsistent measurement criteria, selective disclosure, technical complexity and the absence of a uniform reporting framework were among the key hindrances identified by the respondents. Overall, the findings indicate a gap between investors’ limited knowledge of HRAI and their recognition of its usefulness, highlighting the need for greater consistency, clarity and effective presentation of human resource information in corporate reporting.

title: Isolation-Aware Zeta-Zero Spacings via Signed Fourier Multisets: Variational–Spectral Estimates and Certified Local Blocks (v3.3r1 Research Preprint)
summary: This research preprint consolidates isolation-aware signed Fourier multiset methods, fixed Fourier witnesses, blockwise Gram payments, a single-allocation signed residual framework, and MP9–MP21 proof-first audits for zeta-zero ordinate isolation. It preserves the earlier conditional fifty-mode and wider-spacing bounds and develops a candidate unconditional majority-isolation argument at c=0.1895. Crucially, the end-to-end proof is not yet independently verified; its validity depends on the full-domain analytic reductions, exact directed-interval certificates, arbitrary-multiplicity allocation accounting, smoothing and height transfer, and the BGST–Conrey normalization. The MP21 audit distinguishes quartet kernel positivity through 6c from kernel negativity at 8c in the five-point domain. title: Dynamic Natural-Capital Accounting under Tipping Risk and Spatial Contagion: A Regenerative Forest Network Model
summary: Abstract Classical renewable-resource models value the biological stock that remains after current extraction, whereas ecological resilience theory emphasizes the possibility of alternative regimes separated by tipping boundaries. This paper combines these perspectives in a networked forest-management problem with two continuous ecological states---harvestable biomass and resilience---and a discrete ecological regime for each patch. Harvesting lowers biomass and resilience and increases the endogenous intensity of a harmful regime shift; regenerative effort rebuilds ecological capital and reduces that intensity. The hazard also rises with exposure to degraded neighboring patches, generating spatial contagion. The planner solves an infinite-horizon controlled piecewise-deterministic Markov decision problem. Rather than assuming positive ecological shadow values, we derive them from primitive order conditions by monotone dynamic programming. Six structural results follow. The model nests Clark's classical target-stock problem; sufficiently large expected tipping losses generate \emph{regenerative inactivity}, with zero harvest and positive restoration; the optimal harvest rule contains a direct tipping-risk precautionary wedge; degraded neighbors can induce preventive closure before local collapse; a next-generation matrix yields a spectral threshold for early-stage landscape cascades; and Perron--Frobenius sensitivity identifies the patches at which restoration most effectively reduces systemic ecological risk. A stylized numerical illustration shows how restoration can move a connected forest from a supercritical to a subcritical cascade regime. The framework extends the economics of endogenous regime shifts by making resilience a managed state and by adding network contagion and systemic restoration targeting. JEL codes: C61; Q23; Q28; Q57. title: The Impact of Board Composition on Sustainability Report Readability
summary: This study examines whether and how board composition influences the readability of corporate sustainability reports. Using a sample of 1,334 firm-year observations from S&P 500 companies between 2016 and 2023, we investigate the relationship between board characteristics and report readability while controlling for firm-specific factors. Contrary to conventional wisdom, we find no statistically significant evidence that board-level characteristics, including gender diversity and board size, directly influence sustainability report readability. Our findings suggest that report readability is more likely influenced by operational-level factors than board-level governance structures. These results contribute to the literature on corporate governance and sustainability reporting by challenging existing assumptions about the direct role of board composition in determining reporting quality. Our study has important implications for understanding the mechanisms through which organizational governance affects sustainability disclosure practices.

title: Retail Environmental Responsibility and the Consumer Waste Behaviour Gap: Evidence from South Africa
summary: Abstract Retailers sit between production and household consumption, which makes their environmental corporate social responsibility programmes plausible instruments of behavioural change. Whether customer recognition of those programmes translates into waste management behaviour remains unclear in secondary cities of the global South, where recovery infrastructure is uneven. We surveyed 281 adult customers at two retail complexes in Mbombela, Mpumalanga, South Africa. The questionnaire measured awareness of environmental CSR, information channels, noticed initiatives, perceived effectiveness, perceived influence on waste behaviour, reported household recycling, participation in store led recovery schemes, changes in shopping practice, and barriers to sustainable consumption. We screened the captured data against the permitted response codes, decomposed multiple response items into binary indicators, and used Spearman rank correlations with Benjamini and Hochberg correction for 66 pairwise tests. Awareness was reported by 194 of 279 interpretable respondents, or 69.5%. However, only 75 respondents, or 26.7%, reported recycling household waste, and 147 of 281 reported regular or occasional participation in store led recovery schemes. Among respondents giving an interpretable answer, 187 of 228, or 82.0% believed that retailer initiatives had influenced their waste behaviour. Awareness was associated with perceived influence, but not with household recycling and store scheme participation. Education and age were more consistent correlates of scheme participation, while perceived barriers were more salient among respondents who reported greater engagement. The findings indicate that retailer CSR can be highly visible and persuasive at the level of perception without being sufficient to produce downstream waste behaviour. Consumer communication therefore needs to be coupled to accessible collection, sorting, and recovery systems.

title: Closing the fossil carbon cycle: the Geological Net Zero Pact (FR : Boucler le cycle du carbone fossile : le pacte de Neutralité Géologique en Carbone)
summary: Closing the fossil carbon cycle: the Geological Net Zero Pact. Working version 0.9 Climate disruption results first of all from the transfer of carbon accumulated over millions of years in geological reservoirs into the atmosphere, the ocean and the biosphere, at a pace that natural cycles cannot offset. The Geological Net Zero (GNZ) principle was proposed for COP26 in 2021 and has since been consolidated in the scientific literature. It draws an accounting rule from this: any extraction of fossil carbon must be balanced by a permanent and verified return of carbon to the geosphere. Between COP26 and COP31, the carbon budget compatible with 1.5 °C shrank from 420 to 170 billion tonnes of CO₂. This document reviews that period and explains why a pact between carbon actors is preferable to a resolution imposed from above. It then presents the GNZ Pact: implementation by segments of supply chains, spreading until a critical threshold is reached; its parties and its five commitments; its accounting and the economic model it induces; how it fits with atmospheric CO₂ removal and with fossil fuel transition roadmaps. It ends with a flexible action plan based on demonstrators and verifiable commitments. title: Nine-Dimensional Target Orthodontics (9D-TO): defining the maxillary central incisor target in nine measurable dimensions and auditing ideal, designed and achieved targets
summary: This technical white paper introduces Nine-Dimensional Target Orthodontics (9D-TO), a quantified method for orthodontic treatment planning that starts from the maxillary central incisor (U1). The method has three components:(1) The U1 target is defined in nine measurable dimensions: anteroposterior position, midline, vertical position, torque, incisal cant, rotation, size, growth and patient preference. Each dimension has a stated method, unit, evidence base and tolerance.(2) Every dimension carries three targets: ideal, designed (constrained by bone, incisive canal and space, and confirmed by the clinician) and achieved. All three are measured with a single protocol.(3) The total discrepancy is decomposed into a constraint gap (ideal − designed), an implementation gap (designed − planned set-up) and an execution gap (planned − achieved). The dentition is derived from the U1 target by a chain-based set-up within CBCT bone boundaries. Occlusion is checked on a CBCT-based virtual articulator with clinician-verified landmarks. Key features: quantifiable; auditable; clinician decides; transparent, AI-assisted implementation. The tools were built by a practising dentist with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Anthropic) and Blender. Novelty: to our knowledge, based on a PubMed search on 7 November 2026, no previous work has defined the U1 target in nine measurable dimensions, or decomposed treatment discrepancy into constraint, implementation and execution gaps using a single measurement protocol. This paper introduces the method only; no clinical outcome data are reported. Subsequent technical notes will report the individual modules and their validation. title: Aīthra: Reciprocal Verification for Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) - Exact Cost Laws, Policy Sharing Complexity, and Self-Hosting Experiments
summary: Aīthra develops a mathematical and executable framework for a specific obstacle in recursive self-improvement: making a verifier cheaper for ordinary tasks does not necessarily make it cheaper to evaluate its own proposed successors. Task failures and successor defects can follow different distributions while remaining subject to exactly the same correctness contract. Semantic preservation alone therefore does not establish that an improvement transfers to the next improvement cycle. The central principle is to preserve the meaning of correctness while optimizing how different recursive roles execute that commitment. The work separates semantic admissibility from economic usefulness, quantifies the cost of forcing roles to share one verification policy, and studies when specialization can repay its setup and audit costs. The release combines complete mathematical arguments, a bounded self-hosting prototype, a finite policy-partition formulation, synthetic experiments, and raw reproducibility artifacts. Technical contributions Exact defect transport and hereditary refinement. For a restricted language of mask verifiers, each successor has an exact representation of the obligations it leaves unchecked. Testing that representation with a parent verifier is equivalent to inclusion of the successor’s acceptance set in the parent’s acceptance set. The equivalence also applies to incomplete parents; a complete parent preserves the complete correctness contract in accepted successors. The construction requires the specified verifier language, exact defect extraction, and trusted semantics. An exact law for the cost of policy sharing. In sequential verification with at most one failed obligation, known role identity, and common positive additive test costs, the work derives the expected-work gap between a single optimal shared schedule and separate optimal role schedules. The gap decomposes into opposing pairwise ordering preferences. This characterizes when distinct workload distributions can share an optimal implementation and when their disagreements create a measurable cost. A sharp factor-R bound, where R is the number of roles, quantifies the worst-case sharing penalty; a refinement accounts for calls with no fault. A graph-theoretic characterization and restricted complexity barrier. The minimum number of schedules needed to preserve every role’s optimal expected cost equals the chromatic number of its strict-preference conflict graph, and every finite graph can be realized by the construction. A separate perturbation establishes NP-completeness of bounded-regret sharing with at most three schedules, common unit costs, positive and pairwise-distinct rational singleton-fault probabilities, and a unique optimal schedule for each role. This concerns a specified inverse-polynomial additive-regret decision problem, rather than the complexity of RSI as a whole. Finite optimization of specialization. A subset dynamic program chooses which roles should share policies after incorporating declared policy setup charges. Its recurrence requires O(3^R) work after subset costs are prepared and is suited to small role sets. The theory specifies the exact finite optimization problem; the reference implementation uses floating-point objective accumulation. Oracle distributions, learned source distributions, and actual target performance are kept distinct. Distribution robustness and paid promotion evidence. The framework includes total-variation uncertainty bounds and a fresh paired statistical audit of a fixed candidate. The economic gate accounts for additional setup and realized audit work over a declared deployment horizon. Its analysis requires fresh independent samples, bounded paired costs, and a stationary future target distribution. Correctness comes from the separate semantic contract; the statistical audit evaluates whether a permitted change is worth installing. Executed studies and recorded results The self-hosting study runs 20 independent lineages in a finite 64-obligation verifier domain. The installed executable verifier participates in screening its proposed replacements. Across the recorded runs, 99 changes are accepted, and all lineages reach the known optimum of the finite grammar. Paired controls consume the same candidate tape, isolating the effect of inherited screening. Relative to the frozen improver, the mean reduction in the declared counted-work proxy is 4.97%, with an aggregate reduction of 6.00%. These quantities are not complete CPU-instruction counts. Conventional controls remain stronger: the learned materialization pipeline is slower by median factors of 81.03 against batched NumPy on prepared resident arrays and 1.83 against retained-counterexample checking. The native-screen control also uses less counted work. The prototype demonstrates bounded executable self-application; its proposal distribution remains fixed, and its finite improvement trajectories saturate. A separate 480-trial study evaluates six role-workload families, two common test-cost profiles, six roles, and 48 tests. It includes a distribution-shift failure in which source-trained specialization becomes more expensive than the shared baseline. A subsequent 480-trial study, developed after that negative result and evaluated on new seeds, tests the fresh-audit gate. For the unit-cost conditions, recorded lifecycle savings relative to the learned shared baseline are 54.17% for disjoint roles, 42.25% for paired roles, and 40.07% for rotated roles. These comparisons include declared setup charges, source acquisition, realized audit work, and a horizon of 100,000 deployment calls. Compiler wall time is recorded separately rather than converted into synthetic query-work units. On shifted and mostly-valid workloads, rejected changes still incur audit costs, producing lifecycle savings of −9.62% and −6.98%, respectively. No harmful deployment promotion is observed across the 480 trials of the fresh-audit protocol. This observation applies to the tested protocol and does not establish a universal no-regression guarantee. Validation and reusable artifacts The computational audits include every labeled simple graph on one through five vertices: 1,099 graphs in total. Integer-arithmetic reduction checks, brute-force coloring comparisons, ordering and partition enumeration, exact mask-refinement checks, and independent linear-program comparisons accompany the analytic arguments. These finite checks support the implementation and constructed examples; the general claims rest on the manuscript’s proofs. The research release contains: A 26-page manuscript and editable LaTeX source. Python implementations and synthetic workload generators. Accepted successor programs and complete self-hosting traces. Compact summaries, figures, environment versions, and SHA-256 checksums. 480 role trials, 480 guarded trials, and 21 controlled reversal points. The resulting 981 tabular rows are experiment records, with distinct schemas and documented protocols. The Hugging Face distribution additionally provides a dataset card, typed field dictionary, three loader configurations, and a Windows-compatible dataset uploader. The research computations can be reproduced locally without a GPU, proprietary dataset, model API, or external account once software dependencies are installed. Intended uses include research on verifier evolution, self-modifying programs, metareasoning, verification scheduling, policy specialization, distribution shift, and resource accounting in recursive improvement systems. Scope and attribution The contribution is a scoped mathematical and experimental treatment of verification across recursive roles. Established foundations in scheduling, guessing cost, compatibility clustering, program synthesis, and statistical concentration are credited in the manuscript. Historical priority of the precise restricted formulations remains unresolved. The release does not establish neural-model state of the art or general autonomous RSI. Analytic proofs and executed finite evidence are supplied; external independent replication and proof-assistant formalization are not claimed. title: Exact Minimum-Change Pure Nash Equilibrium Repair in Binary Polymatrix Cactus Games: Source-Complete Separators, Committed Reanchoring, and a Treewidth-Two Complexity Boundary
summary: This preprint develops a structural and algorithmic framework for exact minimum-change pure Nash equilibrium repair in binary polymatrix games on cactus graphs. The problem is to determine whether a pure Nash equilibrium exists within a prescribed Hamming distance of a reference action profile, and to maintain exact repair solutions under local payoff modifications and committed reference changes. The central construction uses source-complete separator interfaces that distinguish joint multi-boundary payoff contributions from one-boundary maximum-support envelopes. Together with a balanced source-token hierarchy and bounded quotient composition rules, these interfaces yield an exact dynamic maintenance algorithm with explicit preprocessing, update, witness extraction, and abstract-space bounds. The paper establishes a worst-case successful-operation bound under a specified abstract arithmetic, indexing, and reference-counted allocation model. It also develops epoch-safe optimization and commit operations, distinguishes equilibrium nonexistence from budget infeasibility, and proves weak NP-hardness of one-edit equilibrium repair on a restricted noncactus family of treewidth-two book graphs. Version 1.7 incorporates corrections arising from adversarial mathematical and source-level audits, including surviving-boundary aggregation, zero-budget witness accounting, deterministic preprocessing, rational bit-space accounting, and history-independent retained-state ownership. A separate reproducibility archive provides executable research implementations, deterministic hierarchy construction, exact-payoff verification, intermediate separator-state comparisons, transactional regression tests, and allocator and memory-reachability audits. The computational evidence supports the mathematical construction but does not constitute universal certification of worst-case physical runtime or garbage-collector behavior. The algorithmic framework also applies to corresponding generic additive-threshold constraint systems; no Nash-specific asymptotic advantage is claimed.
